segments: A developer-founder who owns the product and the marketing site, and hasn't opened the analytics tab since he was forced onto GA4
An independent creator whose site is her livelihood — newsletter, podcast, portfolio — who installed Google Analytics years ago and now dreads opening it
A freelance web designer or small-agency owner carrying analytics for dozens of client sites, who is the person clients ask 'are we compliant?'

business.what_it_does: Fathom shows website owners where visitors come from, which pages they read, and what converts, using a single embed script and a real-time dashboard, without using cookies or tracking visitors individually.
business.business_model: subscription, priced by monthly pageviews across all a customer's sites

facts.statement: EU isolation is enabled by default for every Fathom customer, with no setup required.

provenance.quote: congratulations; as a Fathom customer, you’re already using it, and it’s enabled by default! There’s nothing you have to set up or tweak or even change in your embed script to use it.

facts.statement: Fathom's dashboard is live and real-time; a new visit shows up in the 'Realtime' count.

provenance.quote: Fathom’s dashboard is live and real-time, so the best way to check if our script is installed is by visiting your website and seeing if your visit shows up in the “Realtime” count at the top of your dashboard.

facts.statement: Installation is a single script tag in the site header containing a Site ID.

provenance.quote: <script src="https://cdn.usefathom.com/script.js" data-site="ABCDEFG" defer></script>

facts.statement: Pricing starts at $15/month for up to 100,000 monthly pageviews, rising in tiers to $470/month for up to 25,000,000, with a custom tier above that.

provenance.quote: $15/month Up to 100,000 monthly pageviews ... $470/month Up to 25,000,000 monthly pageviews Custom Over 25,000,000 monthly pageviews

facts.statement: Every plan includes the same analytics features and starts with a 7-day free trial.

provenance.quote: Choose the monthly pageviews you need across all your sites. Every plan includes the same analytics features and starts with a 7-day free trial.

facts.statement: Every plan includes at least 50 sites; extra packs of 50 sites can be added, up to 15 packs, at $10/month or $100/year per pack.

provenance.quote: Every plan includes at least 50 sites, and bigger plans include more. Select a plan above to see exactly how many. If you need more, you can add up to 15 packs of 50 extra sites yourself from your billing settings, at $10/month or $100/year per pack.

facts.statement: There is no free plan; Fathom's business model is selling software rather than monetizing visitor data.

provenance.quote: Do you offer a free plan? Nope, and here’s why: we’ve invested heavily in fast, reliable infrastructure (we don’t host Fathom on cheap servers that go offline). Our business model is selling software, not your data, so we’ve priced Fathom to be sustainable for a very long time.

facts.statement: Fathom does not charge extra for importing historical GA4 data; imported history stays available while the subscription is active.

provenance.source: Import GA4 data into Fathom Analytics
provenance.quote: We don’t charge extra for historical imports. Your imported history stays available to view and export while your Fathom subscription is active.

facts.statement: Pageviews on blocked pages do not count against a plan's pageview allotment.

provenance.quote: Visitors who visit blocked pages do not count as pageviews, so they do not count against your payment plan allotment of pageviews.

facts.statement: Fathom does not do sales calls or live demos as a matter of course; exploration is self-serve via trial, walkthrough video, or live dashboard demo.

provenance.quote: We don’t do sales calls or live demos, but our software is ridiculously easy to use. You can watch our 10-minute walkthrough, click around the live dashboard or give Fathom a 7-day free trial alongside your existing analytics.

facts.statement: Fathom has introduced an AI assistant called Luna.

provenance.quote: Meet Luna, Our AI Assistant

facts.statement: Fathom is positioned primarily for developers and site owners who want GDPR/ePrivacy/PECR/CCPA compliance without cookie consent banners.

entries.claim: Fathom never charges for occasional traffic spikes, doesn't shut off accounts for early limit overages, gives advance email notice and reminders before pausing dashboard/API access for sustained overages, and keeps collecting data throughout.
entries.verbatim: What happens if I go over my pageview limit? We never charge for occasional traffic spikes, and we don't shut your account off if you hit your plan limit early. If you stay well over your limit, we'll email you about a larger plan, and you choose whether to upgrade. We send a few friendly reminders and extra time before we pause dashboard and API access, and we keep collecting your data throughout. See our [plan-limits guide](/docs/account/limits) for the details.

context.subject: Fathom pageview limits
context.conditions: FAQ answer to 'What happens if I go over my pageview limit?'

entries.claim: Fathom never turns off analytics for occasional traffic spikes; for sustained overages it emails about a larger plan, lets the customer choose to upgrade or cancel, sends reminders with extra time before pausing dashboard and API access, and keeps collecting data throughout.

voice.rhythm: Short, declarative sentences strung two or three to a paragraph. Explanations move in simple cause-and-effect steps ("if X, then Y") rather than long subordinate clauses. Paragraphs are compact, usually under four sentences, and features are often summarized in one closing sentence after two of setup.
voice.person: Writes as "we"/"Fathom" (company and product used interchangeably) addressing the reader directly as "you." No individual human signs the copy — it's the company's own voice throughout, not a named person's.
exemplars: Switching analytics doesn’t have to mean starting from zero. Import supported Google Analytics 4 data into your Fathom dashboard, then keep measuring with simple, privacy-focused analytics. We don’t charge extra for historical imports. Fathom shows you what's working on your website without tracking the people who visit it. It's trusted by Fortune 100s, banks, governments and companies of every size. Start with a 7-day free trial, then plans start at $15/month.

If a visitor to your site goes to a blocked page, that pageview will not be tracked. If they’re a current visitor, it’ll show them as still on the previous page (as their view of the new page was blocked). Visitors who visit blocked pages do not count as pageviews, so they do not count against your payment plan allotment of pageviews.

segments.name: A developer-founder who owns the product and the marketing site, and hasn't opened the analytics tab since he was forced onto GA4
segments.situation: He wrote the site, he deploys it, and he is the only person who would notice if the tracking broke. Analytics is item nine on a list of nine: the GA4 property he set up during the Universal Analytics sunset is still technically installed, but he cannot find the answer to 'did the launch post do anything?' in it, so he stopped looking. He knows what his own script budget looks like, because he is the one who gets the PageSpeed complaints, and he knows the consent banner he bolted on is a thing he added to his own site to satisfy a tracker he doesn't even read. People like him in the Laravel/Vue/Alpine orbit talk about Fathom in public — Evan You put it on the Vue.js site because it was lightweight and respected user privacy; James Brooks at Laravel liked that it let them see what they needed right away; Caleb Porzio says that after switching he became more attentive to his sites because he was always aware of who was on them. So he has heard the name, repeatedly, from people he trusts, and still has not put a card down.

situation_provenance.quote: Our new Vue.js website has been using Fathom because I like how it's lightweight and respects user privacy.
Fathom is a beautiful, fast piece of software built on Laravel and it lets us see what we need right away.
After switching to Fathom for my web properties, I find I'm more attentive to my sites because I'm always aware of how many people are on them and which pages are most popular.

segments.job_to_be_done: Know whether the thing he shipped is actually being used, in the ten seconds he can spare between support tickets — and stop being the person who put a surveillance script and a consent pop-up on his own users.
segments.trigger: A question he couldn't answer from the dashboard he has — a launch, a press mention, a post that spiked — or a complaint about page weight and the cookie banner on a site he's proud of.

objections.objection: "Google Analytics is free, Cloudflare's analytics are free, and you're asking me to pay every month, forever, for less data."
objections.answer: The only answer in the evidence is a business-model argument, and it should be used as one rather than dressed up as a feature win. Fathom states plainly that there is no free plan, that it has invested in infrastructure it won't run on cheap servers, and that it sells software rather than visitor data; it acknowledges in the same breath that Cloudflare's analytics are free and that its own product is paid. Its framing of why GA is free (that Google makes enough from the personal data customers hand over) is Fathom's characterisation of a rival, not independent verification. Nothing in the evidence shows that paying produces better or more accurate data than a free tool — so this objection is answered on ethics, sustainability and who owns the data, and is not answered on value-for-money.

provenance.quote: Do you offer a free plan? Nope, and here's why: we've invested heavily in fast, reliable infrastructure (we don't host Fathom on cheap servers that go offline). Our business model is selling software, not your data, so we've priced Fathom to be sustainable for a very long time.

Why isn't Fathom free like Google Analytics? If you aren't paying for a product, you are the product. That's why Google Analytics is free, because they make enough money off the personal data their customers give them by using their analytics service. We charge a small and sustainable fee for Fathom because our business model is selling software, not data. Our customers gladly pay for our service because they know their data is safe with us and their visitors' privacy is protected.

objections.objection: "My site is small. $15/month is $180 a year to learn roughly what I already know, and the cheapest plan is sized for someone with a hundred thousand pageviews I don't have."
objections.answer: Not answered. The lowest tier in the evidence is $15/month for up to 100,000 monthly pageviews, there is no free plan by explicit policy, and nothing in the material offers a hobby, low-traffic or annual-discount entry point below that (the only discount evidence is an unqualified 'Get 2 months free (switch to yearly)' link, with no terms established). All the evidence can do is lower the risk of trying — 7-day trial, card not charged until the trial ends, an email before billing starts, cancel from account settings with no contracts — not the price. For a reader whose traffic is a rounding error against the entry tier, this objection stands and copy should not pretend otherwise; it should sell the 50 sites and the kept history that come with the same $15, or leave this reader alone.

objections.objection: "Switching analytics means starting from zero. I'm not throwing away years of history to get a prettier dashboard."
objections.answer: Largely answerable. Fathom imports supported GA4 data into the dashboard, doesn't charge extra for historical imports, keeps the imported history viewable and exportable while the subscription is active, and the import is a few steps — authorise the Google account, pick the sites, run it — with an email when it finishes. Name the limits before the reader finds them: the importer brings in supported daily analytics available through Google's API and explicitly does not recreate every GA4 report or import GA events, and Universal Analytics data was deleted by Google in July 2024, so anything that lived only there is not recoverable by anyone.

provenance.quote: Can I import Google Analytics into Fathom? Yes. Our [GA importer](/features/ga-importer) brings GA4 data into Fathom so you can keep the history after Google deletes it. The import is done in a privacy-focused way.

objections.objection: "One page of data is too thin. The first real question I ask — where did this cohort drop out of the funnel, what path did that user take — sends me straight back to the tool I was leaving."
objections.answer: Partly answered, and the unanswered part is structural. On the yes side: the single-page dashboard is a deliberate design choice against tools with twelve sections and seventy-plus reports; it covers live and total visitors, pageviews, top pages, referrers, countries, devices, browsers, events and UTM campaigns; filters drill into a campaign, country or single page in a click; saved views and date comparisons persist the questions you ask repeatedly; events carry a monetary value and currency so conversions and revenue sit beside pageviews; Search Console adds search terms, clicks, impressions and positions; and CSV export plus the Analytics API let you take the data elsewhere. On the no side: nothing in the evidence offers funnels, cohort analysis, session recordings or individual user journeys, and Fathom states it does not track individuals and anonymises with hashes and salts — so per-person paths are not a missing feature, they are precluded by the design. A reader who genuinely needs funnels should not be told otherwise.

provenance.quote: That's why our dashboard is a single page of data. It's manageable, without metrics most website owners don't need or care about.

objections.objection: "Our reporting runs through Google — Ads, BigQuery, Looker. Analytics that doesn't plug into the ad platforms breaks our attribution, whatever else it does."
objections.answer: Not answered. There is nothing in the evidence about Google Ads integration, conversion import back to ad platforms, BigQuery export or BI connectors. The closest the material gets is UTM tagging to tell newsletters, ads and social campaigns apart with campaign-level filtering, Google Search Console linkage, and CSV export plus an Analytics API on every plan — plus the fact that Fathom can be run alongside existing analytics during the trial, which is a way to defer the decision rather than resolve it. For a buyer whose job is managing paid spend, this objection cannot be beaten with what we currently know.

objections.objection: "Our policy is that EU visitor data stays in the EU. You're a Canadian company storing analytics on US infrastructure."
objections.answer: Strongly answerable for most buyers, with one caveat to state rather than hide. EU isolation is on by default for every customer on every plan with nothing to set up, EU visitor traffic is routed through European-owned infrastructure, the IP address — personal data under GDPR — is stripped inside the EU and never reaches US infrastructure, EU servers are in Falkenstein, Helsinki and Nuremberg, the UK, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein are treated as EU, Canada is covered by the EU adequacy decision, privacy lawyers vetted how data is collected and stored, and the feature was built with EU legal experts. For a hard EU-only mandate, the honest position is that anonymised analytics are stored on US servers by default, and the route to all-traffic-through-the-EU is Extreme EU Isolation via the cdn-eu script URL. Everything here is Fathom's own statement; the EU-only comparison claim and the 'up to 50% faster than EU-only infrastructure' figure are the vendor's framing with no methodology given.

provenance.quote: Why is Fathom better than European-only providers? Our [data isolation](/features/data-isolation) routes EU visitor traffic through EU infrastructure. Visitors elsewhere are routed through our global infrastructure, so they can connect closer to home. This helps keep analytics fast for visitors around the world.

objections.objection: "Procurement needs a signed DPA, a SOC 2 or ISO report, a sub-processor list and a pen test. I can't buy on a vendor's assurance that lawyers looked at it."
objections.answer: Not answered. The evidence contains compliance assertions — GDPR, CCPA, ePrivacy, PECR 'and more' — a statement that privacy lawyers vetted how data is collected and stored, that Data Isolation was built in collaboration with EU legal experts, that Canada is covered by the EU adequacy decision, and one named sub-processor (Bunny.net as the EU-owned CDN). There is no independent audit, certification, attestation, DPA or security report anywhere in the ledger, and no sales call or live demo is available to walk a security reviewer through it. For an enterprise or regulated buyer this is a dead end with current knowledge; the logo wall (Microsoft, IBM, GitHub, NYT, banks and governments as unnamed categories) is logo-only attribution and will not survive a security questionnaire.

objections.objection: "You won't even get on a call, and I have to hand over a card just to look around. Seven days is not an evaluation."
objections.answer: Partly answered, and the gap is deliberate on Fathom's side. Fathom states outright that it doesn't do sales calls or live demos, and offers instead a 10-minute dashboard walkthrough video, a live demo dashboard you can click around without signing up, full documentation and email support from real humans. On the card: the trial is 7 days, the card isn't charged until it ends, Fathom emails before billing starts, cancellation is self-serve in account settings with no contracts, and the trial can be run alongside existing analytics — plus install is verifiable in minutes because the dashboard is real-time, so the evaluation starts the same day rather than on day three. What the evidence does not offer is a longer trial, an extension, or any human walkthrough for a buyer who needs to bring colleagues along.

provenance.quote: Can I explore Fathom before signing up? We don't do sales calls or live demos, but our software is ridiculously easy to use. You can watch our [10-minute walkthrough](/video/dashboard-walkthrough), click around the [live dashboard](https://app.usefathom.com/demo) or give Fathom a 7-day free trial alongside your existing analytics. Every feature is [documented](/docs), and if you have specific questions, we're here by [email](/about/contact).

objections.objection: "Pricing by pageviews means a good month costs me money, or my dashboard gets switched off mid-launch."
objections.answer: Answerable, and the policy is unusually specific. Occasional traffic spikes are never charged for, accounts aren't shut off on first hitting a limit, and for sustained overage Fathom emails about a larger plan, sends several reminders plus extra time before pausing dashboard and API access, and keeps collecting data throughout. Tier changes need two consecutive months over the limit before Fathom gets in touch, and two consecutive months under before you can move down yourself from billing settings. Pageviews are pooled across all sites, and traffic you block — blocked pages, and local, staging and test environments excluded via allowed domains — does not count against the allotment. One cost to disclose rather than bury: custom events, whether fired on the site or sent through the API, each count towards the monthly pageview allowance, so heavy event tracking consumes the plan.

provenance.quote: What happens if I hit my pageview limit? We'll never turn your analytics off for occasional traffic spikes. If you stay well over your limit, we'll email you about a larger plan, and you decide whether to upgrade or cancel (no hard feelings either way). We send a few friendly reminders and extra time before we pause dashboard and API access, and we keep collecting your data throughout. See our [plan-limits guide](/docs/account/limits) for the details.

objections.objection: "I'd rather self-host — Matomo or similar on a box I control, data genuinely mine, no monthly bill."
objections.answer: Partly answered, and the first half must be conceded: Fathom cannot be self-hosted, and says so directly, because it processes pageviews on a global CDN and EU visitor data in the EU. What the evidence offers against self-hosting is work avoided and vendor-claimed comparisons: GDPR compliance with no setup or knowledge required, by default on every plan, versus a self-hosted tool whose GDPR manager and IP anonymisation need configuration and knowledge to use correctly; cookie consent still required unless several steps are taken; a GA import that needs an API key generated in Google Cloud's console; your own CDN to host the script for comparable global speed; a 20KB-plus script against a few-KB deferred one; and a hosted/cloud retention cap of 24 months against retention for as long as you're a customer. Every one of those comparisons is Fathom's own characterisation of a rival, not independent verification — do not present it as a benchmark.

provenance.quote: Can I host the data locally? No. Fathom is a hosted product so we can process pageviews on a global CDN, keep dashboards fast, and process EU visitor data in the EU. Everyone else is routed to the closest region.

objections.objection: "My history only exists while I keep paying, and cancelling queues it for deletion. That's lock-in — from a two-person bootstrapped company I'd be trusting with a decade of data."
objections.answer: Half answered. Exit is real and self-serve: data can be exported from the day you started until now, even decades of it, via CSV download or the Analytics API, exports and email reports are unlimited on every plan, and you can export before cancelling with no contracts and no phone call. But the terms are exactly as the objection states — retention is forever only as long as you are a paying customer, and cancellation queues the data for deletion, with the obligation to export sitting on the customer. On vendor durability, the evidence says Fathom is independent and bootstrapped with no VC, bank loans or outside shareholders and was started by two creators; that is the whole of it. Nothing in the evidence speaks to business continuity, escrow or what happens to data if Fathom stops operating, so the 'what if you fold' half of this objection cannot be beaten with what we know.

objections.objection: "I'd have to get into the site's head tag, and my developer is booked for weeks — or it's me and I'd rather not touch the template."
objections.answer: Fully answerable. Installation is one line of JavaScript in the header — a script tag pointing at cdn.usefathom.com/script.js with your Site ID and defer — or an integration if you'd rather not touch templates; the WordPress route needs no template editing at all, and there are documented integrations for WordPress, Ghost, Webflow, Next.js, Nuxt, Vue, Gatsby, Drupal, Carrd, Discourse and more. Because the dashboard is real-time, verification is visiting your own site and watching the Realtime count move. Nothing here requires a sprint ticket.

objections.objection: "How would I know the numbers are even real? My last dashboard was full of bot referrals and my own visits."
objections.answer: Answerable. Bots, crawlers, DDoS junk and other non-human traffic are filtered out so the dashboard reflects people who actually visited, with automatic bot filtering on every plan, and data appears in real time rather than a day or two later. The site firewall blocks or allows by page, IP (including IPv4 wildcards), referrer, domain, country and event name, and allowed domains filter out any hostname not on the list, including local, staging and test environments. Your own visits can be excluded by IP, or per-browser by running fathom.blockTrackingForMe() in the console, or by honouring DNT. Spam already in the reports is removed through Data removals in the site's Manage settings — the firewall only stops future visits. Note that an empty block or allow list filters nothing, and a tight allow list of exact event names will silently drop dynamically named events.

provenance.quote: How do I opt out of being counted? Fathom doesn't track individuals. We anonymise data with [hashes and salts](/docs/troubleshooting/hashes-salts). If you still don't want your own visits on a dashboard, [block your IP](/docs/script/firewall#ip) or run a small script from your browser console. You can also set Fathom to [honour DNT](/docs/script/script-advanced#dnt).

map.summary: 7 audience(s) mapped; 0 worth exploring first. Commercial priority is a hypothesis, not a response-rate forecast.
map.validation_note: Product requirements rechecked against current Knowledge in one closed-world call. Audience identities and market evidence are retained; market sources were not refetched.
map.reading:
Assessment summary. Verified quotations do not establish demand or purchase intent; commercial priority remains a hypothesis.
- A technical founder who built the site himself and gave up on GA4 somewhere around the third Explore report: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence limited (2 quoted source(s)); use or purchase captured; reachability venue identified.
- The person at a European company who has been told, by someone with authority, that Google Analytics has to go: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence limited (3 quoted source(s)); use or purchase unknown; reachability venue identified.
- A clinic group or telehealth startup rebuilding its public marketing site after the tracking-pixel settlements: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence limited (1 quoted source(s)); use or purchase unknown; reachability venue identified.
- A small nonprofit or advocacy site whose visitors would be endangered by ad-tech trackers: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence limited (2 quoted source(s)); use or purchase unknown; reachability venue identified.
- A freelancer or small studio who installs analytics on every client site and gets asked for the numbers by people who will never log in: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence absent (1 quoted source(s)); use or purchase unknown; reachability venue identified.
- A US business that just received a CIPA 'wiretapping' demand letter naming the scripts on its website: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence limited (1 quoted source(s)); use or purchase unknown; reachability unknown.
- A small EU-selling ecommerce brand whose consent banner is eating a third of its own sales data: hypothesis; product compatibility supported; audience evidence limited (3 quoted source(s)); use or purchase unknown; reachability unknown.
map.note: Coverage gaps and failures: (1) Direct buyer-voice forum threads were hard to surface — three attempts at Reddit and Hacker News practitioner threads on freelance multi-client analytics and Ghost/newsletter publishers returned vendor comparison pages instead, so the freelancer segment leans on the existence of a reporting-tool market rather than quoted complaints. (2) No churn evidence found: searches for people who left or cancelled Fathom turned up only review-site remarks that it is 'expensive for what you get' and costs more per pageview than Plausible past 1M views, with no first-person account — real churn reasons remain unknown. (3) Security posture unverified: a search for Fathom Analytics SOC 2/BAA returned results for an unrelated AI meeting-notes company also called Fathom, so treat any certification claim as unconfirmed and do not reuse those hits. (4) No named EU public-sector or university procurement decision was found, so the institutional variant of the compliance buyer is unsupported and was not proposed as a separate segment. (5) Search scope was left empty, so no geography was imposed; German-language vocabulary was tried once and returned agency listicles rather than buyer discussion. (6) Population counts are unknown throughout, fit is left at zero, and assessment fields are left at defaults for separate validation. (7) The Shopify candidate has no documented install path in the supplied capability catalogue — verify before using it. (8) One source (clickport) is a vendor-adjacent guide and one (levelup) is a practitioner essay; both should be read as advocacy, and the consent-loss percentages they cite differ widely and need independent checking.

reasons: OpenCage — a small, founder-run geocoding API business whose engineer writes the stack posts — publicly documents stopping Google Analytics and paying for Fathom, which is both usage and a stated paid relationship from a member of this exact segment.

problem_fits.caveat: The problem's sources are dated 2018-2023, so the GA4 click-depth complaint is not corroborated as current.
problem_fits.why: Documented capability is a single page of data shown in real time, which is the structural opposite of multi-screen report navigation.

problem_fits.caveat: Fathom's own characterisation; cookie-consent requirements vary by jurisdiction and the compliance list is self-declared with no third-party audit referenced.
problem_fits.why: The no-cookies mechanism is documented and the no-banner conclusion is stated on official and vendor pages for the audience's most corroborated problem.

problem_fits.caveat: The selected evidence documents a one-line install and pre-built integrations but states no setup time or effort measurement; the problem is single-source and undated.
problem_fits.why: Install is one script tag or a pre-built integration and verification is looking at the realtime count, which is the no-coding path this founder asked for.

problem_fits.caveat: The specific counter-claim, that IP and user-agent processing alone triggers a consent requirement, is not answered by the selected evidence: anonymisation is asserted but its mechanism is not established here, and all compliance statements are the vendor's own.
problem_fits.why: No cookies, fewer data points, anonymisation and controller-only personal-data processing are licensed, but they narrow rather than settle the dispute.

segment_objections.objection: No cookies does not remove a consent obligation; the tool still sees IP and user agent, so some jurisdictions still require a popup.
segment_objections.answer: Fathom does not use cookies at all, collects fewer data points and anonymises personal data, processes personal data only for its own controller purposes, and states GDPR, CCPA, ePrivacy and PECR compliance; the ledger also records that consent requirements vary by jurisdiction and that this compliance is self-declared, so the anonymisation mechanism itself is not established by the selected evidence.

segment_objections.objection: Google Analytics is free; why pay for analytics on a small founder site?
segment_objections.answer: Pricing starts at $15/month for up to 100,000 monthly pageviews with cancel-anytime terms, and every plan includes the same analytics features, so the entry tier is not a reduced product.

segment_objections.objection: There is no free tier and the trial wants a card up front.
segment_objections.answer: The trial is 7 days, the card is not charged until it ends, Fathom emails before billing starts, the subscription can be cancelled in account settings, and Fathom can run alongside existing analytics during the trial.

segment_objections.objection: I would rather self-host an open-source tool on a cheap VPS and keep the data myself.
segment_objections.answer: The selected evidence does not establish any self-hosted Fathom option, so that preference is not met; what it does license is that a comparable privacy setup in Matomo requires setup and knowledge to be used correctly, while Fathom is a single line of code that runs on any site, app or CMS.

segment_objections.objection: Switching means losing my Google Analytics history.
segment_objections.answer: The GA4 importer brings in supported daily analytics from Google's API but does not recreate every GA4 report or import GA events, and it cannot recover Universal Analytics data Google deleted in July 2024; data collected in Fathom is kept and exportable for as long as you remain a customer.

allowed_claims: EU isolation is enabled by default for every Fathom customer, with nothing to set up.
No changes to the embed script are needed to use EU isolation.
Fathom automatically routes data from EU visitors to be processed in the EU, and data from all other visitors to be processed in the US.
EU isolation treats visitors from Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom as EU for data-routing purposes, even though they are non-EU member nations.
Fathom's EU servers are located in Falkenstein, Helsinki, and Nuremberg.
Extreme EU Isolation routes all global traffic through the EU by using the script URL https://cdn-eu.usefathom.com/script.js instead of the default embed script.
Firewall settings are adjusted by going to Settings, then Sites, clicking the site, then clicking the Firewall tab.
The site firewall offers six list tabs to configure: Pages, IPs, Referrers, Domains, Countries, and Events.
Blocking pages, IPs, domains, or countries in the firewall does not restrict visitor access to the site; it only prevents those visits from appearing in the Fathom dashboard.
Page blocking supports wildcards, such as /about/*, to block all pages under a given path (e.g. /about/team, /about/luna).
IP blocking supports wildcard patterns, e.g. 100.100.100.* blocks any IP starting with 100.100.100., such as 100.100.100.1 and 100.100.100.123.
Only IPv4 addresses are currently supported for wildcard IP blocking.
Blocking a country in the firewall keeps that country's visitors able to view the website while excluding their pageviews and analytics data from showing up in Fathom.
Referrer blocking supports wildcards, e.g. *.example.com blocks all subdomains of example.com as referrers.
Once one or more allowed domains are added to the Domains firewall list, data coming from any other domain is blocked instantly.
Wildcard domain entries like *.example.com in the allowed domains list cover subdomains (e.g. subdomain.example.com, www.example.com) but do not allow the root domain example.com itself.
The Events firewall tab can drop junk/unwanted event names at collect time, or restrict collection to only the names sent on purpose.

In the Events firewall, Block mode drops the listed event names while still collecting every other event; Allow mode collects only the listed names/wildcard patterns, and an empty allow list collects every event.
For dynamic event names (for example Shopify product titles), an Events allow list needs a wildcard such as 'Product *'; a tight allow list of exact names will drop those dynamic events.
The firewall only stops future visits; existing spam already in reports must be cleaned up using Data removals in the site's Manage settings.
Fathom's tracking script can be installed via Fathom's WordPress plugin or one of Fathom's other integrations, placed in the header of the site's code.
Fathom's dashboard is live and real-time, so script installation can be verified by checking whether a visit shows up in the 'Realtime' count at the top of the dashboard.
Fathom provides a browser console command, fathom.blockTrackingForMe(), that blocks tracking for the current browser on a page where Fathom is installed.
The blockTrackingForMe setting is stored in the browser's local storage, so it continues working for future visits from that browser.
Fathom's embed script is a single script tag, <script src="https://cdn.usefathom.com/script.js" data-site="ABCDEFG" defer></script>, with the Site ID as the data-site attribute.
The Site ID is a short, unique code that identifies the site, needed for the tracking snippet, integrations, and API calls.
Fathom's advanced script settings support ignoring canonicals, honouring DNT (Do Not Track), and single-page applications (SPAs), among other options.
EU visitors' personal data stays in the EU while Fathom's anonymized analytics are stored on its US infrastructure.
Fathom customers do not need to show cookie notices.
Fathom's EU Cloud is monitored 24/7, is highly available and multi-region, and is available to all customers on all plans.
Every Fathom plan, including the smallest, includes Data Isolation, enabled by default.
Fathom's Data Isolation method works by intelligently routing visitors to the right place to process their data.

For visitors inside the EU, Fathom's CDN routes the pageview to European servers that strip the IP address before it reaches US infrastructure, and the resulting anonymous data is stored on US servers with zero personal data attached.
Fathom can import supported Google Analytics 4 data into the Fathom dashboard.
Fathom does not charge extra for historical GA4 imports.
Fathom's GA4 importer brings in supported daily analytics available through Google's API, but does not recreate every GA4 report or import GA events.
Imported GA4 data has different filtering options from data collected natively by Fathom, and totals can differ between the two tools.
Large GA4 imports may require smaller date ranges.
Fathom measures website activity without analytics cookies or cross-site advertising profiles.

Fathom provides email reports.
Fathom lets users make their dashboard public.

Fathom Analytics offers a full dashboard demo video that is about 8 minutes long.
Fathom Analytics' embed code is minimal (just a few KB) and loads deferred so it doesn't hurt your PageSpeed score.
Fathom Analytics loads its script via its own CDN so it loads quickly whether you're in Europe or anywhere else in the world.
Using Fathom Analytics doesn't hurt your SEO.
Fathom Analytics collects fewer data points than Matomo and anonymizes that personal data.
Fathom Analytics' embed code doesn't use cookies and was built from the start to focus on compliance with GDPR and other privacy laws.
Fathom anonymizes visitors' IP addresses by default.
Fathom anonymizes URLs with personal identifiers in URL parameters by default.
Fathom doesn't use cookies, ever.
Fathom anonymizes precise location data from the full IP address by default.
Fathom never tracks keystrokes on forms on your site.

Fathom doesn't use cookies, so visitors don't need a consent/cookie banner for analytics.
Fathom filters out bots, crawlers, DDoS junk and other non-human traffic so the dashboard shows only people who actually visited.
Fathom shows data in real time, not 24 to 48 hours later.

Fathom's dashboard shows which pages are popular, who's sending traffic, which campaigns are converting and which events are paying off, all from one dashboard, and a filter lets users drill into a campaign, a country or a single page in a click.
Users can combine filters, name the view and reopen it in one click, and everyone with access to that site can use the same saved views.
Users can mark a launch, a redesign or a press mention on the traffic chart with a milestone.

Fathom uses UTM tags to tell newsletters, ads and social campaigns apart, and the dashboard can be filtered by a campaign to see its traffic, the pages people visited and the events they completed.

Users can schedule weekly or monthly email reports for themselves, colleagues or clients, send a report for one website or bring several sites together in the same email, and each recipient gets only the sites selected for them.
Users can check all their sites together in the all-sites view, then open a site for details, and can share individual dashboards publicly or protect them with a password.
Fathom data can be downloaded as CSV files for a spreadsheet or report, or accessed via Fathom's API to bring data into other tools.
Fathom can import historical GA4 data.
Fathom can be used with WordPress, Ghost, Webflow, Next.js, Nuxt and plenty more, added via one line of JavaScript or a pre-built integration.
Fathom's tracking script is small and loads asynchronously, so it doesn't hold up the rest of the page.
Fathom is built to handle traffic spikes and large websites.
Fathom's anonymisation methods are documented, and EU visitor data is handled with data isolation.
Fathom is a hosted product that processes pageviews on a global CDN, processes EU visitor data in the EU, and routes everyone else to the closest region.
Fathom doesn't track individuals and anonymises data with hashes and salts.
Users who don't want their own visits on a dashboard can block their IP or run a small script from their browser console, and can also set Fathom to honour DNT (Do Not Track).

Fathom provides email support from real humans on every plan.

problem_fits.caveat: The problem's sources are dated 2018-2023, so the GA4 click-depth complaint is not corroborated as current.
problem_fits.why: Documented capability is a single page of data shown in real time, which is the structural opposite of multi-screen report navigation.

problem_fits.caveat: Fathom's own characterisation; cookie-consent requirements vary by jurisdiction and the compliance list is self-declared with no third-party audit referenced.
problem_fits.why: The no-cookies mechanism is documented and the no-banner conclusion is stated on official and vendor pages for the audience's most corroborated problem.

problem_fits.caveat: The selected evidence documents a one-line install and pre-built integrations but states no setup time or effort measurement; the problem is single-source and undated.
problem_fits.why: Install is one script tag or a pre-built integration and verification is looking at the realtime count, which is the no-coding path this founder asked for.

problem_fits.caveat: The specific counter-claim, that IP and user-agent processing alone triggers a consent requirement, is not answered by the selected evidence: anonymisation is asserted but its mechanism is not established here, and all compliance statements are the vendor's own.
problem_fits.why: No cookies, fewer data points, anonymisation and controller-only personal-data processing are licensed, but they narrow rather than settle the dispute.

segment_objections.objection: No cookies does not remove a consent obligation; the tool still sees IP and user agent, so some jurisdictions still require a popup.
segment_objections.answer: Fathom does not use cookies at all, collects fewer data points and anonymises personal data, processes personal data only for its own controller purposes, and states GDPR, CCPA, ePrivacy and PECR compliance; the ledger also records that consent requirements vary by jurisdiction and that this compliance is self-declared, so the anonymisation mechanism itself is not established by the selected evidence.

segment_objections.objection: Google Analytics is free; why pay for analytics on a small founder site?
segment_objections.answer: Pricing starts at $15/month for up to 100,000 monthly pageviews with cancel-anytime terms, and every plan includes the same analytics features, so the entry tier is not a reduced product.

segment_objections.objection: There is no free tier and the trial wants a card up front.
segment_objections.answer: The trial is 7 days, the card is not charged until it ends, Fathom emails before billing starts, the subscription can be cancelled in account settings, and Fathom can run alongside existing analytics during the trial.

segment_objections.objection: I would rather self-host an open-source tool on a cheap VPS and keep the data myself.
segment_objections.answer: The selected evidence does not establish any self-hosted Fathom option, so that preference is not met; what it does license is that a comparable privacy setup in Matomo requires setup and knowledge to be used correctly, while Fathom is a single line of code that runs on any site, app or CMS.

allowed_claims: EU isolation is enabled by default for every Fathom customer, with nothing to set up.
No changes to the embed script are needed to use EU isolation.
Fathom automatically routes data from EU visitors to be processed in the EU, and data from all other visitors to be processed in the US.
EU isolation treats visitors from Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom as EU for data-routing purposes, even though they are non-EU member nations.
Fathom's EU servers are located in Falkenstein, Helsinki, and Nuremberg.
Extreme EU Isolation routes all global traffic through the EU by using the script URL https://cdn-eu.usefathom.com/script.js instead of the default embed script.
Firewall settings are adjusted by going to Settings, then Sites, clicking the site, then clicking the Firewall tab.
The site firewall offers six list tabs to configure: Pages, IPs, Referrers, Domains, Countries, and Events.
Blocking pages, IPs, domains, or countries in the firewall does not restrict visitor access to the site; it only prevents those visits from appearing in the Fathom dashboard.
Page blocking supports wildcards, such as /about/*, to block all pages under a given path (e.g. /about/team, /about/luna).
IP blocking supports wildcard patterns, e.g. 100.100.100.* blocks any IP starting with 100.100.100., such as 100.100.100.1 and 100.100.100.123.
Only IPv4 addresses are currently supported for wildcard IP blocking.
Blocking a country in the firewall keeps that country's visitors able to view the website while excluding their pageviews and analytics data from showing up in Fathom.
Referrer blocking supports wildcards, e.g. *.example.com blocks all subdomains of example.com as referrers.
Once one or more allowed domains are added to the Domains firewall list, data coming from any other domain is blocked instantly.
Wildcard domain entries like *.example.com in the allowed domains list cover subdomains (e.g. subdomain.example.com, www.example.com) but do not allow the root domain example.com itself.
The Events firewall tab can drop junk/unwanted event names at collect time, or restrict collection to only the names sent on purpose.

In the Events firewall, Block mode drops the listed event names while still collecting every other event; Allow mode collects only the listed names/wildcard patterns, and an empty allow list collects every event.
For dynamic event names (for example Shopify product titles), an Events allow list needs a wildcard such as 'Product *'; a tight allow list of exact names will drop those dynamic events.
The firewall only stops future visits; existing spam already in reports must be cleaned up using Data removals in the site's Manage settings.
Fathom's tracking script can be installed via Fathom's WordPress plugin or one of Fathom's other integrations, placed in the header of the site's code.
Fathom's dashboard is live and real-time, so script installation can be verified by checking whether a visit shows up in the 'Realtime' count at the top of the dashboard.
Fathom provides a browser console command, fathom.blockTrackingForMe(), that blocks tracking for the current browser on a page where Fathom is installed.
The blockTrackingForMe setting is stored in the browser's local storage, so it continues working for future visits from that browser.
Fathom's embed script is a single script tag, <script src="https://cdn.usefathom.com/script.js" data-site="ABCDEFG" defer></script>, with the Site ID as the data-site attribute.
The Site ID is a short, unique code that identifies the site, needed for the tracking snippet, integrations, and API calls.
Fathom's advanced script settings support ignoring canonicals, honouring DNT (Do Not Track), and single-page applications (SPAs), among other options.
EU visitors' personal data stays in the EU while Fathom's anonymized analytics are stored on its US infrastructure.
